introduction: This is a guide of warnings. It speaks of recompense for individuals and for peoples, of kings and divines called to account, of those who waited for a promised day and denied it when it came, and of the heedless; and it explains punishment less as a penalty imposed than as a loss, remoteness from what one was made for. A hundred of its quotations are read here with a hundred from elsewhere. The same warnings fill the older scriptures: what is sown is reaped, the writing appears on the wall, the tyrant spreads like a green tree and is gone, a city does not know the time of its visitation. So do the same mercies: God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, does not afflict willingly, delays so that people may turn, and embraces all things. Milton, Khayyam, Emerson and the Dhammapada describe a requital that is within the act itself. The difficulties are placed where they belong. Job and the man born blind suffer without having earned it; the Preacher and Jeremiah see the wicked prosper; Voltaire refuses to read an earthquake as a sentence; Hardy and Ivan Karamazov refuse the scheme altogether. A reader of these passages should hear both the warning and the questions honest people have always put to it.
questions: The guide speaks of retribution for individuals and for whole peoples. What makes it legitimate, or dangerous, to read a people's suffering as requital, as Lincoln did and Voltaire would not?
Punishment is described here as deprivation and remoteness. How does that differ from a penalty imposed from outside, and which of the outside voices says something similar?
Job, the man born blind and those under the tower in Siloam suffered without being worse than others. What place do the guide's warnings leave for suffering that is not chastisement?
The psalmist envied the wicked, and the Preacher noticed that sentence is slow. What is delay for, according to Peter, Ezekiel and the Qur'an?
Many of these passages address rulers and religious leaders. Why are those with authority warned more severely?
The Qur'an says that mercy embraces all things in the same breath as it speaks of punishment. How would you hold the two together when speaking to someone who fears God's anger?

outside.why: Paul states the rule of individual recompense: whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
Lincoln read a nation's war as collective requital: every drop of blood drawn with the lash might be paid by another drawn with the sword.
Voltaire asked whether more vice was found in fallen Lisbon than in Paris, where voluptuous joys abound. When is it right, and when wrong, to read a people's calamity as retribution?
Moses sets life and death, blessing and cursing, before the people, and says: therefore choose life.
The Qur'an says that the truth is from the Lord: whosoever will, let him believe, and whosoever will, let him disbelieve.
The psalm says that the Lord is slow to anger and has not dealt with us after our sins.
The Qur'an says that a good deed receives tenfold the like, and an ill deed only the like of it.
Paul quotes a call to the sleeper: awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead.
Isaiah hears one God say: I form the light and create darkness, I make peace and create evil. If reward and chastisement have a single source, what becomes of the idea of a second power?
John's Gospel says of an earlier coming that he came unto his own, and his own received him not.
Jesus charges religious teachers with shutting up the kingdom of heaven against others, neither going in themselves nor letting others enter.
Jesus weeps over a city that did not know the time of its visitation.
Jesus warns that false Christs and false prophets shall arise and show great signs and wonders.
John's letter tells believers not to believe every spirit, but to try the spirits whether they are of God.
Jesus speaks of those who build the tombs of the prophets and say that in their fathers' days they would not have joined in.
Jesus laments over Jerusalem: how often would I have gathered thy children together, and ye would not.
Jesus compares the last days to the days of Noah, when they ate and drank and married until the flood came.
Jeremiah hears that if a nation turn from its evil, God will repent of the evil he thought to do unto it. Is a warning of chastisement a prediction or an appeal?
Jonah cries that in forty days Nineveh shall be overthrown, and the people of Nineveh believe and proclaim a fast.

Jesus denies that those on whom the tower in Siloam fell were sinners above others, and adds: except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. How does he both refuse and keep the link between sin and disaster?
The Qur'an says that most people follow nothing but conjecture, which can by no means take the place of truth.
Isaiah pronounces woe on them that decree unrighteous decrees, to turn aside the needy from judgment.
Socrates says that if he must choose he would rather suffer injustice than do it. Who, in the guide's account of an unjust sentence, is the more to be pitied?
Daniel reads the writing on a king's wall: God hath numbered thy kingdom and finished it; thou art weighed in the balances.
Shelley's traveller finds the boast of a king of kings on a pedestal, and round it the lone and level sands.
The Qur'an recalls how the Lord dealt with A'ad, Thamud and Pharaoh, and says: thy Lord is ever watchful.
The psalmist has seen the wicked in great power, spreading like a green bay tree, and then he was not.
Thucydides records the doctrine that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. Is the fall of tyrants a law of history, or a hope?
Shakespeare's king says that within the hollow crown that rounds the temples of a king, Death keeps his court.
John's Gospel defines the condemnation: light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light.
In Revelation the souls of the slain cry with a loud voice: how long, O Lord?
Jeremiah pleads with God about his judgments: wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper?
Jeremiah blames counsellors who healed the people's hurt slightly, saying peace, peace, when there is no peace.
Isaiah says that iniquities have separated between the people and their God, and hid his face from them.
In the parable the torment is a distance: between us and you there is a great gulf fixed.
Milton's fallen angel says that the mind is its own place and can make a heaven of hell, a hell of heaven. Is deprivation a punishment that any change of mind could undo?
The Qur'an says that no laden soul bears another's load, and that God never punishes until a messenger has been sent.
Ezekiel hears God swear that he has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn and live.
Khayyam's soul returns from the Invisible to answer 'I myself am Heaven and Hell'. If hell is a condition of the soul, is it any the less real?
The Dhammapada says that pain follows an evil thought as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage.
Paul writes that the trumpet shall sound and the dead shall be raised, in the twinkling of an eye.
Jesus says that the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear, and they that hear shall live.
Revelation tells those about to suffer not to fear, and to be faithful.
The Qur'an says that whoso does an atom's weight of good will see it.
Emerson says that crime and punishment grow out of one stem, punishment ripening unsuspected within the flower of the pleasure.
The psalm says that man's days are as grass: the wind passes over it, and the place thereof shall know it no more.
Isaiah compares the wicked to the troubled sea when it cannot rest, and says there is no peace for them.

Job, having lost everything, says the Lord gave and the Lord hath taken away, and blesses his name. Is his suffering a torment of either kind, and what does it do to the rule that torment follows wrong?
Paul calls godliness with contentment great gain, since we brought nothing into this world and can carry nothing out.

The Preacher saw just men to whom it happens according to the work of the wicked, and wicked men to whom it happens according to the work of the righteous. What does a promise of contentment say to that?
Acts says that God has made of one blood all nations of men to dwell on all the face of the earth.
Jefferson trembled for his country when he reflected that God is just, and that his justice cannot sleep for ever.
Jesus warns that salt which has lost its savour is good for nothing but to be cast out.
Jesus says that every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation.
Obadiah states the rule of return: as thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee.
Exodus speaks of iniquity visited upon the children unto the third and fourth generation. How far do the consequences of a wrong travel, and is that the same as punishment?
The rich man in the parable tells his soul to take its ease, and is told: this night thy soul shall be required of thee.
Revelation hears a mighty cry over a great city: Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen.
Jesus says that whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones shall in no wise lose his reward.
In the parable the tares are left to grow with the wheat until the harvest. Why might requital be delayed, and what is the delay for?
Paul says that the invisible things are clearly seen from what is made, so that people are without excuse.
Paul promises that in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Jeremiah hears the Lord ask whether any can hide himself in secret places and not be seen.
The Dhammapada says there is no spot in the sky, the sea or the clefts of the mountains where one might be freed from an evil deed.
The Preacher observes that because sentence is not executed speedily, hearts are fully set to do evil. Why is requital so often slow, and what does the delay test?
The psalmist admits that he was envious when he saw the prosperity of the wicked. What is honest in that envy, and what answers it?
Micah says that what is required is to do justly, to love mercy and to walk humbly with thy God.
In the parable of judgment what was done or not done to the hungry, the stranger and the sick is counted as done to the judge.
The psalm promises that they that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
In Luke the blessings on those who weep now are followed by woes on those who laugh now.
Jesus tells his disciples to watch and pray, for the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak.
Jesus says that with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again.
A saying of Muhammad holds that the reward of deeds depends upon the intentions.
Moses wishes that the people were wise and would consider their latter end.
Lamentations says that the Lord does not afflict willingly, nor grieve the children of men.
Paul forbids his readers to avenge themselves: vengeance is mine, I will repay, saith the Lord. What does leaving requital to God ask of the injured?
Peter's letter recalls one who, when he was reviled, reviled not again, but committed himself to him that judges righteously.
Ivan Karamazov finds the price asked for harmony too high and hastens to give back his ticket. Does the promise that the wicked will be punished answer him, or is it part of what he refuses?
Jesus says that he must work while it is day, for the night comes when no man can work.
Proverbs says that the simple believe every word, but the prudent look well to their going.
The psalm advises: fret not thyself because of evildoers, for they shall soon be cut down like the grass.
The Qur'an says that whatever misfortune strikes is what your own hands have earned, and that He forgives much.
Hardy finds no avenger behind his losses, only Crass Casualty and dicing Time. Is a world with requital easier to live in than a world of chance?
In the parable the servant who has gained five talents more comes to give his account.
In the Qur'an God says: I smite with my punishment whom I will, and my mercy embraceth all things. How do the two halves of that sentence stand together?
The psalm says that the Lord is good to all, and his tender mercies are over all his works.
Peter's letter explains delay as patience: the Lord is longsuffering, not willing that any should perish.
The Qur'an says that if God took mankind to task by what they deserve, no living creature would be left, but he reprieves them to an appointed term.
Ezekiel says that when the wicked man turns away from his wickedness he shall save his soul alive.
Paul asks whether his reader despises the goodness and forbearance of God, not knowing that it leads to repentance.
Isaiah's complaint against his own people is that the ox knows his owner, but they do not consider.
Hebrews tells its readers not to despise the chastening of the Lord, for whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth.
Judges tells of a generation gathered to their fathers, and another arising that knew not the Lord nor his works.
Ezekiel says that the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father that of the son.
Asked whose sin caused a man to be born blind, his own or his parents', Jesus answers neither. How much suffering is not requital at all?
A dying man is promised paradise that same day. If a moment's delay can void a lifetime's deeds, can a moment's turning redeem one?
The Qur'an tells those who have been prodigal to their own hurt not to despair of the mercy of God, who forgives all sins.
The Qur'an says that corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what men's hands have done.
Jesus says that unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.
Jesus calls blessed the eyes that see what many prophets and righteous men desired to see and did not.

proverbs-diggeth-a-pit.text: Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him

romans-according-to-his-deeds.text: Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance? But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God; Who will render to every man according to his deeds

ezekiel-no-pleasure-in-the-death-of-the-.text: Say unto them, As I live, saith the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel

hebrews-whom-the-lord-loveth-he-chastene.text: My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when thou art rebuked of him: For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth

lamentations-doth-not-afflict-willingly.text: For the Lord will not cast off for ever: But though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies. For he doth not afflict willingly nor grieve the children of men

ecclesiastes-just-men-work-of-the-wicked.text: There is a vanity which is done upon the earth; that there be just men, unto whom it happeneth according to the work of the wicked; again, there be wicked men, to whom it happeneth according to the work of the righteous: I said that this also is vanity

isaiah-no-peace-unto-the-wicked.text: But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt. There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked

proverbs-way-of-transgressors-is-hard.text: Good understanding giveth favour: but the way of transgressors is hard

isaiah-iniquities-have-separated.text: But your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you, that he will not hear

quran-thy-lord-is-ever-watchful.text: Dost thou not consider how thy Lord dealt with (the tribe of) A'ad, With many-columned Iram, The like of which was not created in the lands; And with (the tribe of) Thamud, who clove the rocks in the valley; And with Pharaoh, firm of might, Who (all) were rebellious (to Allah) in these lands, And multiplied iniquity therein? Therefore thy Lord poured on them the disaster of His punishment. Lo! thy Lord is ever watchful

quran-never-punish-until-a-messenger.text: Whosoever goeth right, it is only for (the good of) his own soul that he goeth right, and whosoever erreth, erreth only to its hurt. No laden soul can bear another's load, We never punish until we have sent a messenger.

quran-if-allah-took-mankind-to-task.text: If Allah took mankind to task by that which they deserve, He would not leave a living creature on the surface of the earth; but He reprieveth them unto an appointed term, and when their term cometh - then verily (they will know that) Allah is ever Seer of His slaves.

quran-good-deed-tenfold.text: Whoso bringeth a good deed will receive tenfold the like thereof, while whoso bringeth an ill-deed will be awarded but the like thereof; and they will not be wronged.

quran-whosoever-will-let-him-believe.text: Say: (It is) the truth from the Lord of you (all). Then whosoever will, let him believe, and whosoever will, let him disbelieve. Lo! We have prepared for disbelievers Fire. Its tent encloseth them. If they ask for showers, they will be showered with water like to molten lead which burneth the faces. Calamitous the drink and ill the resting-place!

dhammapada-not-in-the-sky.text: Not in the sky, not in the midst of the sea, not if we enter into the clefts of the mountains, is there known a spot in the whole world where a man might be freed from an evil deed

shakespeare-bloody-instructions.text: we but teach / Bloody instructions, which, being taught, return / To plague the inventor

shakespeare-the-gods-are-just.text: The gods are just, and of our pleasant vices / Make instruments to plague us
shakespeare-the-gods-are-just.author: William Shakespeare

psalm-until-i-understood-their-end.text: When I thought to know this, it was too painful for me; Until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end

psalm-envious-at-the-foolish.text: For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked

lincoln-judgments-of-the-lord.text: Yet, if God wills that it continue until all the wealth piled by the bondman's two hundred and fifty years of unrequited toil shall be sunk, and until every drop of blood drawn with the lash shall be paid by another drawn with the sword, as was said three thousand years ago, so still it must be said, "The judgments of the Lord are true and righteous altogether
lincoln-judgments-of-the-lord.author: Abraham Lincoln

emerson-crime-and-punishment-one-stem.text: Crime and punishment grow out of one stem. Punishment is a fruit that unsuspected ripens within the flower of the pleasure which concealed it
emerson-crime-and-punishment-one-stem.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
